analysis.one_liner: Replaces the estate tax with an optional 1% income surtax paid over at least seven years, and repeals the tax on generation-skipping trusts
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2015 with two cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let anyone elect, while alive, to stop paying estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes at death and instead pay an extra 1% of their annual income for a minimum of seven years. Anyone who dies within seven years of electing still owes the estate tax, minus a credit for surtax already paid. In exchange, heirs would lose the 'step-up' in basis that today erases tax on a lifetime of unrealized gains at death, and instead owe capital gains tax when they sell inherited property.
analysis.who_benefits: The owners of the very largest estates. Today the estate tax applies only above a multi-million-dollar exemption at a 40% rate on amounts above it; the bill's own findings note that in 2012 only about 9,400 estate tax returns were even required to be filed. For a family with most of its wealth in low-basis assets and a modest annual income, a 1% surtax on income for seven years is a small fraction of a 40% tax on the whole estate. Ending the generation-skipping transfer tax also benefits dynasty trusts designed to pass wealth across generations untaxed. Family-owned businesses and farms are the bill's stated beneficiaries, and some would gain, but the population actually subject to the tax is small.

how_it_helps.text: Electors would stop owing estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes at death, replacing them with a 1% annual surtax on modified adjusted gross income for at least seven taxable years [S2][S3].
The bill's stated purpose is to stop the estate tax from forcing family farms, ranches, and businesses to be sold to pay the tax, which the findings say causes job losses and dislocation [S3].

The findings argue the current estate tax costs wealthy families compliance expenses roughly equal to what it raises for the Treasury, and drives capital into trusts where it sits idle, so the swap is pitched as a simplification that frees capital [S3].

Heirs would no longer enjoy the step-up in basis: inherited property would carry the decedent's original basis, and gains would be taxed as capital gains when heirs sell, with new information-return and reporting requirements to enforce that [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, which the bill's own findings say collected $14 billion from the estate tax in fiscal 2013 — roughly 1% of IRS collections — and, ultimately, other taxpayers who would have to make that up or see deficits rise. Heirs of electing decedents would also bear a new capital gains tax on inherited appreciation when they sell, though deferral until sale makes it cheaper than the estate tax it replaces.

drawbacks.text: A decedent who dies within seven years of electing owes the estate tax anyway, with only a partial credit for surtax paid, so the election is a bet on longevity that penalizes short-lived electors [S3].

The bill's own findings claim the swap would be revenue neutral, but the mechanism does not guarantee it: the surtax is 1% of annual income, and the largest estates typically hold wealth in low-basis assets that generate little reported income, so dynastic wealth could pay far less under the surtax than under the 40% estate tax, with the deferral built into carry-over basis softening even that [S3].

The new carry-over basis regime creates a real compliance burden: executors must file detailed returns within 180 days of death and heirs must file annual reports on inherited property, with penalties of $10,000, $5,000, or $250 per failure for skipping them [S3].

Running the old and new systems side by side — with elections, transition clawbacks, credits for taxes paid, and a two-year window for revoking trusts tax-free — adds its own complexity to a code the bill says is already too complicated [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief is real but concentrated: a handful of the largest estates each year, plus some farm and business owners, would owe dramatically less at death. The offsetting costs — forgone revenue the bill's own findings peg at $14 billion in a single year, new basis-reporting burdens on heirs, and a dual system that adds rather than removes complexity for anyone straddling the two regimes — land broadly on other taxpayers and executors. The strongest honest case for the bill is administrative simplification; the design does not reliably deliver the revenue neutrality its findings promise.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Representative Andy Harris introduced the bill on September 15, 2015, joined by Representatives Alex Mooney of West Virginia and Don Beyer of Virginia [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed, and the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury and the general taxpayer base, who continue to receive the roughly $14 billion a year the estate tax raises rather than absorbing the bill's shift of that burden. The wealthiest estates the bill was designed for gained nothing, but lost nothing either, since the current tax was unchanged.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — one Republican and one Democrat joined the Republican sponsor — but no committee or floor vote ever occurred, so there is no record of who would have supported or opposed it.

industries.industry: Holders of very large estates and dynasty trusts
industries.note: Ending the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes is a direct tax cut for the multi-million-dollar estates and multigenerational trusts that are the only ones subject to them; the 1% income surtax and carry-over basis only partly claw that back. Their gain comes out of Treasury revenue that other taxpayers would otherwise not have to cover.

The bill's stated beneficiaries: owners who would otherwise face selling a going concern to cover the tax. The gain is real for those affected, though the bill's own figures show the tax touches only a small number of returns each year, and the largest estates capture most of the total relief.

industries.industry: Trust and estate planning and administration services
industries.note: The findings say compliance costs roughly equal the tax's revenue yield, so eliminating the estate tax would remove much of that business — but the bill replaces it with new basis-reporting duties for executors and heirs, backed by penalties of $10,000 or more per failure.
